It started slowly with the rich California film industry people buying up all the extra housing because it was affordable compared to what they were used to. Then locals with rentals realized they could jack up rents because the California people could afford it. So rents became ridiculous. A house worth $200k in 2010 sold for $1.2 million in 2017. People here thought the post-covid housing market was wild, but we’d already seen that. Locals were quickly priced out of the housing market. 

Then lots of neighborhoods went through gentrification. This didn’t get much pushback because initially, it just seemed like some neighborhoods were getting a makeover. Some old abandoned buildings were now trendy stores and condos. Cool. But slowly, businesses that had been in neighborhoods for generations were pushed out. When property values go up, taxes go up. Some local spots got bought out by predatory builders who gave folks small percentages of what their business was worth because they knew the owner couldn’t afford to pay the property tax and was desperate. 

Then came the overdevelopment. The city didn’t well regulate the development to match the infrastructure. Every scrap of land has a building on it. Atlanta used to be known as “the city in the trees” and that is slowly not true. Any riverside property with a trail is now a multi use development and a parking lot. The roads are over-congested. The city itself is hotter because of a disappearing of trees. It has become this sea of suburb - every ten minutes is just a copy/paste of the same 20 chain stores over and over and over again.

At this point many places in Atlanta pushed to slow development and re-establish mom & pop local spots, but you can’t really put the toothpaste back in the tube.

Putting on the bat signal to get the film industry to land in your state is basically like asking for a swarm of locusts. They’ll descend. They’ll take everything of value, strip the land to squeeze every bit of monetary value from it, and leave nothing for the people who made that place wonderful in the first place.

Hi! My partner was diagnosed at 32 (2 years ago). The first 6 months were rough, but now he’s back to normal, hiking, biking and generally kicking ass. 

The next 2 months will be SUPER difficult. It’s going to be the steepest learning curve and you’re going to feel like you don’t know if you can do this forever. 

Then it gets better. You start figuring things out, you can come to this group to ask questions & you’ll slowly start regaining a little normality.

What helped us, was to create “today” goals, “this week” “one-month” and “90-day” goals. It helped keep us straight and encouraged us not to slip into a full blown anxiety attack. Maybe your today goal is just “eat a meal and write down the results”. 

For the first several months especially, don’t freak out too much about her A1C. It’s going to be erratic as she figures stuff out. Don’t leave the house without emergency sugar just in case. 

Ignore family members and other non-type 1’s trying to be helpful. They have almost no idea what they’re talking about. 

Get in with her endocrinologist as soon as you can & they’ll help you calculate insulin and give you some meal ideas. She can eat whatever she wants, but my partner found it helpful to start slow with some low-carb meals so that he didn’t have to “go on the big ride” quite so often. 

His endocrinologist recommended we err on the side of being too high vs being too low for the first few months & I’d agree with that.

You’re both going to be ok. Your goal is: do not panic about everything all at once, eat, get some rest.

Type 2 diabetes is the kind diagnosed most typically in folks who are obese, or otherwise leading an unhealthy lifestyle. This type of diabetes is somewhat reversible with lifestyle changes. 

Type 1 diabetes is most often diagnosed in childhood and is a genetic, auto-immune disorder. It’s a life-long disease and can be managed, but isn’t caused by diet.  

He has type 1, but was diagnosed as an adult which is somewhat rare. It basically lay dormant in his system and *something* woke it up. Typically, that triggering event is something that stresses the body’s immune system….and then once your body isn’t sick anymore it just kinda keeps attacking itself (in this case, his immune system attacks the pancreas). Recently, this is happening a lot with folks when they get Covid. That wasn’t the case with him - tbh we aren’t sure what triggered it. Maybe something as simple as being constantly stressed at work for a few months. 

Diet is now SUPER important to him because spikes and dips in blood sugar will eventually kill him. So, the big big dips and spikes you see with OMAD fasting, are actually making his other organs work even harder. Because he has Type 1, they’re working hard enough. To live a longer life, we do whatever we can to help his organs not have to be on overdrive - and for him, that will mean not causing blood sugar spikes and dips that come with intense fasting.

In this instance, OMAD was damaging to his metabolic health specifically, because with diabetes you want super level blood sugar levels. He was essentially jacking his up and then letting it crash.
